title: Zomkom
author: Fafa Gilbert
desc: Three hundred grams of millet flour, a litre of water and five hundred millilitres of fermented whey, spiced with cloves, ginger and dried chillies.
longDesc: Zomkom is the millet drink of northern Ghana, synonymous with northerners by its author's own description. This version keeps it simple: three hundred grams of millet flour to a litre of water and five hundred millilitres of fermented whey, with ten cloves, fifty grams of ginger, five dried chillies and a hundred grams of honey or sugar. Evaporated milk or natural yoghurt is optional. The whey is bought already fermented, so no fermentation is carried out — she offers a three-day millet soak as an alternative route, and that option is refused here for having no endpoint.
ingredients: 100 ml evaporated milk, or natural yoghurt (optional)
steps: // The published method for this recipe is video-only. No written steps exist in the source.
Grind the cloves, ginger and dried chillies.
Mix the millet flour with the spices.
Whisk in the litre of water to a smooth slurry.
Cook briefly, stirring, if a cooked base is wanted.
Sweeten with the honey or sugar.
Add the evaporated milk or yoghurt if using, and serve cold.
// The order above is inferred from the documented northern millet drinks, not from this source.
chefTips: The fermented whey is bought, not made — which is what makes this version publishable. Her alternative route, soaking whole millet three days, carries no endpoint and is not followed here.
Ten cloves and fifty grams of ginger for six servings is a strong spicing, and it is what distinguishes zomkom from a plain millet drink.
Grind the spices with the millet rather than steeping them. That is the documented practice for the related drinks.
Five dried chillies in a sweet milky drink sounds wrong and is correct. The heat sits behind the sweetness.
Serve cold. This is a hot-weather drink and it is sold from coolers.
Be aware the method here is reconstructed. The author publishes a full ingredient list and no written steps.

An older documented northern relative, fula, is quite different — steamed millet balls pounded with pepper and cloves, then mashed into water or milk with sugar. If this recipe seems thin, that is the fuller tradition behind it.
commonMistakes: Attempting the three-day millet soak without an endpoint to judge it by.
Steeping the spices instead of grinding them in.
Treating the reconstructed step order as the author's own.
sources: Quantities from 'Zomkoum', byline as printed 'Fafa Gilbert', 31 January 2021. Quantities confirmed across two fetches (TWO-PASS). Her note: zomkom is 'synonymous with the Northerners from Ghana'.

Ingredients exactly as printed: 300g of Millet flour; 1 litre of Water; 500ml of fermented Whey; 10 Cloves; 50g of Ginger; 5 dried Chillies; 100g of Honey or Sugar; 100ml of Evaporated Milk (optional) or natural Yoghurt.

METHOD GAP, stated plainly: THE METHOD IS VIDEO ONLY. No written steps and no cue of any kind. The steps in this entry are explicitly marked as reconstructed from the documented northern millet drinks, and the step list carries a header saying so.

FERMENTATION, and why this entry is publishable where the fuller version is not: the FERMENTED WHEY IS A BOUGHT INGREDIENT, so no fermentation is carried out in this recipe. The author offers an alternative — 'You can use whole Millet that has been soaked for 3 days (to allow fermentation to take place)' — and THAT OPTION IS REFUSED under this collection's fermentation rule: three days with no observable cue. The whey's own fermentation is also unspecified. The published recipe is therefore the assembly, with the ferment bought in.

THE OLDER AND FULLER NORTHERN RELATIVE, from Whitby 1968, which does NOT use the name zomkom but describes the closest Ghanaian match under 'Fula', verbatim: 'The millet is soaked and pounded to remove husks which are winnowed off. It is then ground to flour which is mixed with water to a dough and shaped into balls. These are put into a large container with yam vines or other support in the bottom to hold them above the level of the boiling water and are steamed for about one hour in the covered vessel. The dough is then removed and pounded gently in a mortar. Pepper and ground cloves (kanafuri, masoro) are added bit by bit until completely mixed. The dough is then shaped into balls again and rolled in rice or milled flour... The balls are mashed into water or milk; sugar is added and so eaten.' NOTE the shared spicing — pepper and cloves — across sixty years.
A WRITTEN GHANAIAN ZOMKOM RECIPE WITH A METHOD: EMPTY. This is the only acceptable source with quantities, and it has no method.

SOURCES REJECTED, named as requested: bintghade.com, byline 'mabrurah', whose recipe adds bananas, coconut and dates; theonlinecook.com, byline the site's own name, with unit-less lines such as '5 Ginger' and '½ Sugar' and a page date of October 2026; and BusinessGhana, byline the site's own name, with no quantities.

FOR COMPARISON ONLY, and NOT Ghana — the only zoom-koom paper with real endpoints, from Burkina Faso: Tapsoba F.W., Sawadogo-Lingani H., Kabore D., Compaore-Sereme D., Dicko M.H., African Journal of Microbiology Research, 2017. Soaking: 'soaked in a quantity of water equal to twice of the mass of millet', 16 h. Flavourings '3 g/100 g for the mint and 6 g/100 g for the ginger' (SINGLE-PASS). 'The dough is left to stand for fermentation for 10 h (average time observed in the field)', ambient 33-42 °C at Zogona. pH start to end with titratable acidity: Zogona millet 5.7 to 4.1 (TA 0.45 to 0.71 g/100g); Zogona red sorghum 6.2 to 4.2 (0.15 to 0.49); Dassasgho millet 5.7 to 4.2 (0.37 to 0.90); Dassasgho red sorghum 5.8 to 4.6 (0.13 to 0.45). A TEMPERATURE DISAGREEMENT WITHIN THAT PAPER'S OWN EXTRACTION: one pass gave Dassasgho as 'approximately 33°C' and the other as '21-22°C'. Also recorded: Côte d'Ivoire street zoom-koom (Wognin et al., International Journal of Biosciences 22(2), 2023, SINGLE-PASS) at pH 3.5-4.27, TA 1.6-3.54 g/L. NONE OF THIS IS GHANAIAN and none is used to supply this recipe's endpoint — it is recorded to show that the endpoint exists in the literature for the regional drink, just not for Ghana.
NO YIELD is printed. The six servings above is an editorial reading of 1.5 litres of total liquid.
storage: 2 days refrigerated. It separates and needs shaking.
healthBenefits: Millet is gluten-free and higher in iron and magnesium than maize.
Fermented whey supplies lactic acid bacteria and protein.
Ginger and cloves both carry documented antimicrobial compounds.
Hydrating and filling at once, which is why it is a working drink.
culturalNote: Zomkom is sold in bags and bottles across northern Ghana and it is a meal as much as a drink — millet, spice, whey and sugar, cold, in the middle of a hot day. The older fula tradition behind it involved steaming millet balls for an hour before pounding them, which tells you how much labour the modern flour version removes.
